assertions.text: The mapping from traveller category and ticket type to which discount applies is not in the same table as the count → percentage ladder, and the ladder consumes a count it does not itself derive. Judge this as a property of the decomposition, not as a fixed table count: a solution using four or more tables PASSES provided both conditions hold, and adding a table that covers a further dimension is never a failure here. FAILS when one table both decides the discount by traveller category and maps counts to percentages, or when the ladder table derives its own count from a raw history.

All three discount outcomes appear as distinct expectations somewhere in the class: no discount for a period ticket, a flat 20% for a child single ticket, and a ladder-derived percentage for an adult/senior single ticket. Judge wherever each is stated — they need not share a table, and no particular table name is required.

The mapping from traveller category and ticket type to which discount scheme applies is derived in one table. FAILS when a sibling table repeats traveller-category rows to re-derive it. A solution need not name a 'scheme' concept and must not be rewarded for doing so — what is judged is that the mapping is derived in a single place.

Children's flat 20% discount is represented — as a row wherever the discount that applies is decided, or a separate note. It does not follow the ladder. Judge wherever that rule is stated, not in a table with a particular name.

The discount ladder has multiple tiers derived from the 'every fifth trip' rule, with boundary values or value sets showing which ticket counts produce which discount. The maximum 40% discount is represented.
The 30-day rolling window boundary is tested: a ticket at exactly 30 days is included, at 31 days is excluded.

The 30-day window is exercised at time-of-purchase granularity, not whole days only. The requirement says the count is 'measured at the time of purchase', so at least one pair of rows must distinguish just-inside from just-outside by less than a day (e.g. 29 days 23 hours ago counts, 30 days 1 hour ago does not). A table whose finest distinction is whole days (30 vs 31) FAILS, however many boundary rows it has.

A past purchase that is not a single ticket is shown by row not to count toward the travel count. FAILS when period tickets appear only where the discount for the purchase being made is decided, and never in the rule that decides whether a past purchase counts. Judge wherever countability is decided, not in a table with a particular name.

A table takes a purchase history and produces a travel count, and at least one of its histories contains both counting and non-counting purchases. FAILS when every count the ladder consumes is supplied as a bare number and no table derives one from a history.
Value sets in the tier table contain exactly the values that produce the same discount. No cross-tier contamination.

The discount ladder table uses value sets for the ticket count column to group counts within the same tier (e.g. {5, 6, 7, 8, 9} or {5, 9} for min/max → 5%) — not one row per boundary value. The 'every fifth trip' rule creates tiers; the table should express tiers, not enumerate boundaries.

The tier-to-discount mapping is expressed once — not repeated across multiple tables. A price application table (if present) should test the arithmetic (base price × discount → final price) without re-enumerating which ticket counts map to which tier.

Where the ticket being bought enters its own travel count is visible on the published surface — a column name, a @DisplayName or a @Description — not only in a method body. Either placement is correct: the count may include the purchase being made, or the ladder may apply the +1. FAILS when a count table yields 0 for an empty history and the ladder maps a count of 5 to 5%, because the +1 is then stated nowhere and the two tables cannot be joined by a reader.
@DisplayName is present on test methods, OR method names read as clear descriptive titles when converted from camelCase/snake_case.

@Description is present on at least the class or the tier method and provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as the discount ladder structure, eligibility rules, or application context. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show.
Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.

Wherever the discount percentage is decided, a Zone column (or equivalent) carries a value set showing that the discount applies regardless of zone — rather than silently omitting zone. The requirement explicitly says 'regardless of the zones you travel in'. Judge wherever that rule is stated, not in a table with a particular name. This is about the percentage, not about counting, which zone-independent-counting covers.

The rolling-window counting concern shows by row that a past purchase's zone does not affect whether it counts toward the travel count — for example history entries whose zones differ (or a zone value set) reaching the same count. The claim must be exercised by data: stating it only in @Description, or fixing every history entry to a single zone in the test or a converter, FAILS. This is about counting, not about the discount percentage, which zone-irrelevance-visible covers.

Adult and senior are expressed as a value set {ADULT, SENIOR} (or equivalent) in at least one row wherever traveller category appears, since they follow identical discount rules. Not enumerated as separate rows with the same outcome. Judge wherever traveller category is stated, not in a table with a particular name.

All 9 discount tiers are represented in the ladder table: 0% (tickets 1-4), 5% (5-9), 10% (10-14), 15% (15-19), 20% (20-24), 25% (25-29), 30% (30-34), 35% (35-39), and 40% (40+). Not just a subset of tiers.

Each tier in the discount ladder is expressed as a single row with a value set for ticket counts — not split across multiple rows (e.g. separate rows for 'tier kicks in' and 'tier holds'). One tier = one row.

The rolling window table expresses time relatively (e.g. '14 days ago', '30 days ago', or an integer 'Days ago' column) rather than using absolute dates, making the table readable without needing to know the reference date.

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.

Judge each @TableTest in isolation. The assertion FAILS if a row re-covers an obligation an earlier row in the SAME table already discharged (e.g. a full region x speed x weight cross-product where one row per rate band would state the same rule). Judge each table against its concern's coverage obligations — the distinct behaviours the rule must demonstrate. Where the expected output states those obligations for a concern, judge against that list and do not invent a stricter one; where it does not, derive them from the concern itself. A row that discharges an obligation no other row reaches earns its place however simple it looks, and a value set that covers several values in one row is the preferred discharge, never a failure. ROWS YOU THINK ARE MISSING ARE NEVER A FAILURE HERE — this assertion judges excess rows only, and coverage is judged by 2.19-covers-every-tier and quantifier-covered-by-rows. Judge every @TableTest method in the class; your evidence must name each method with PASS or FAIL.

Judge the class as a whole. The assertion FAILS if a whole @TableTest re-proves rules that earlier tables already established — an integration or end-to-end table whose rows re-prove established rules is the common case, and it fails however clean the other tables are. Sibling tables that each isolate one rule are NOT duplication merely because they share a baseline row: four surcharge tables that each show 'no surcharge' then 'surcharge applied' are four legitimate tables, not one duplicated four times. Collapsing several same-fixture tables into one, as concern-not-over-split requires, is likewise not a failure here. Rows you think are missing are never a failure here. Your evidence must name the re-proving table and the table it duplicates.
The build file (build.gradle) includes org.tabletest:tabletest-junit as a test dependency

Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Do not fail a table merely because its values are simple or round — only these three conditions matter. One exemption applies to conditions (1) and (3): a table whose claim IS an invariance — that some input does not affect the outcome — correctly holds one expectation value across every row, because that constant is the rule's subject rather than evidence of a weak table. A single row varying that input over a value set (e.g. '{DHL, UPS, FEDEX} | 12.00') is the correct compact form and PASSES, provided the title or description states the invariance. Condition (2) is not exempted.

A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone; (3) a helper method used in the assertion applies a comparison criterion (ordering, tolerance, subset matching) that is stated nowhere in the table, title, or description. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Setup that merely constructs the objects named by the columns is not a failure. Judge every @TableTest method in the class. Your evidence must list each method name with PASS or FAIL beside it; a verdict reported from a subset of the methods is not a verdict. A value counts as published if it appears ANYWHERE on the test class's published surface: any @DisplayName or @Description on any method, the class-level @Description, or a column of any table. A method with no @DisplayName publishes its own name as its title, with camelCase split into words, so method names count as published text. Clause (1) triggers only when the value appears ONLY in the method body or a field — a value stated in a sibling method's @Description is published, not hidden.

Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails. Judge ONLY the title — the @DisplayName, or the method name it falls back to. The @Description and the scenario names are other assertions' subject; a description that restates a domain rule is not this assertion's failure and must not be cited as one.
The generated test code compiles successfully against the project scaffolding

A value the rule's outcome depends on, and which the table holds constant for every row, must be visible as a column or named in the @DisplayName/@Description as deliberately held fixed. It must not sit silently in the test method body or a field. Readers generalise from what varies, so an unstated constant is read as part of the rule: a table whose every row happens to use one traveller category states, to its reader, a rule about that category. FAILS when the method body, a field, or a @TypeConverter fixes a value that (1) the outcome depends on, and (2) appears in no column and is not named in the title or description as held fixed. A value declared only in a source-code comment (// or /* */) FAILS: the published surface is the title, the description and the table, and a comment reaches none of them. A method with no @DisplayName publishes its own name as its title, with camelCase split into words, so a constant named in the method name is declared. PASSES when every such constant is either a column or declared. Values that cannot affect the outcome are not failures — a fixed clock used only to construct inputs, object identity, or fixture values the rule is indifferent to. Declaring a held constant in @Description is NOT redundancy and does not conflict with the description-* assertions: those forbid restating what the rows already show, whereas a held constant is precisely what the rows cannot show.

When a title or description quantifies over a domain — 'regardless of X', 'any X', 'whatever the X', 'with or without X' — the rows must actually cover that domain. A value set discharges the promise and is the preferred way to do so: one row holding {A, B, C} both covers the domain and states the independence. Additional near-identical rows are NOT required and are NOT credited. FAILS when a quantifying claim appears and the tables show only one value of the quantified domain, or fewer values than the claim needs (e.g. 'regardless of category' with a single category anywhere in the table). PASSES when the quantified values appear, whether as a value set in one row or as separate rows; also passes when no quantifying claim is made. This assertion is about the claim matching the rows, NOT about row count. Satisfying it by adding rows where a value set would do is not an improvement and must not be scored as one, and it never requires cross-multiplying two quantified domains.
